question: Recently, practices used by Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution have come to light, raising serious concerns about compliance with democratic principles and procedures that are governed by the rule of law. This includes the surveillance of opposition politicians without their knowledge, with the individuals concerned having no opportunity to seek a judicial review of the measures.
The former head of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution was also monitored by Office1, apparently at a time he was planning to set up a new party. 1.

With EU law and democratic principles in mind, what is the Commission’s view of the actions of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution in monitoring opposition politicians without expressly informing them?
With EU law in mind, what is the Commission’s view of the German Government’s treatment of opposition parties?
What measures does the Commission recommend to ensure compliance with democratic principles and procedures governed by the rule of law in the Member States?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.4.2024) The Commission has a firm stance when it comes to promoting democracy including free and fair elections. On 3 December 2020, it published its European Democracy Action Plan1.

It has made the protection of key democratic pillars a political priority and has sought to set out a reinforced EU policy framework to promote free and fair elections and strong democratic participation. While the Commission monitors developments in the Member States, it does not have a general competence to intervene in the elections of Member States.

Subject to the respect of certain basic principles, such as those laid down in Articles 2 and 10 of the Treaty on European Union, and their international commitments, it is the competence and the responsibility of the Member States to lay down the specific conditions for the conduct of elections, and of the competent national administrative and judicial authorities to ensure compliance with applicable law and relevant international standards.

In December 2023, the Commission published a Recommendation on inclusive and resilient elections as part of the Defence of Democracy Package. The Recommendation stresses that surveillance and spyware tools should not be used to interfere with the democratic debate, notably by targeting political actors and journalists.

It considers that while there may be instances whereby spyware is used to defend national security, its use to gain a political advantage can never be justified as a national security matter. Member States are encouraged to facilitate citizen electoral observers in the electoral process.

No later than one year after the next elections to the European Parliament, the Commission will assess the impact of the Recommendation in the Commission’s Report on the elections to the European Parliament.
